Cape Canaveral SLC-41, 2016-09-08. OSIRIS-REx (Origins, Spectral Interpretation, Resource Identification, Security — Regolith Explorer) was the first US asteroid sample-return mission. Designed to study a primordial carbonaceous asteroid that may preserve material from the early solar system.
Centaur upper stage burn places OSIRIS-REx on a heliocentric trajectory pre-tuned to use an Earth gravity assist 1 year later for the energy required to match Bennu's inclination.

2017-09-22. Closest approach 17,237 km over Antarctica. The 8.2°-inclination kick rotated OSIRIS-REx's orbital plane to match Bennu's 6° inclination — the assist did the heavy lifting that propellant alone couldn't have.
First approach-phase burn. Slows OSIRIS-REx to match Bennu's heliocentric velocity for rendezvous.
2018-12-03. OSIRIS-REx arrives at 492-m-diameter Bennu — a carbonaceous near-Earth asteroid. Stationkeeping at 19 km, then orbital characterization.

Sequence of approach burns place OSIRIS-REx into a 1.4-km circumnavigation — the closest-ever spacecraft orbit around a celestial body. Surveyed Bennu for about two and a half years, mapping the boulder-strewn surface in unprecedented detail. Discovered active particle ejections from the asteroid — a previously unknown class of behaviour.

2020-10-20. OSIRIS-REx descended to the Nightingale site, fired a burst of N₂ gas into the surface from its sample-collection arm, and grabbed a sample-rich plume — then immediately backed away. The asteroid surface turned out to be 'rubble-pile fluid' — the spacecraft sank ~50 cm into the surface in the few seconds it was in contact. Sample mass returned: 121.6 g, the largest asteroid sample ever.
2021-05-10. Departure burn places OSIRIS-REx onto a 2.5-year heliocentric trajectory back toward Earth for sample drop.

2023-09-24. Sample Return Capsule (SRC) released at 102,000 km, entered the atmosphere at 12.4 km/s, parachuted into the Utah Test and Training Range. The spacecraft itself was immediately redesignated OSIRIS-APEX and rerouted toward asteroid Apophis, which passes about 32,000 km from Earth on 2029-04-13; OSIRIS-APEX arrives later that month.
Largest asteroid sample ever returned (121.6 g of Bennu, delivered to Earth 2023-09-24)

OSIRIS-REx carried out one of the most exacting asteroid-proximity operations ever attempted. Launched 2016-09-08 from Cape Canaveral on an Atlas V 411, used a 2017 Earth gravity assist to rotate its orbital plane onto Bennu's 6° inclination, and rendezvoused with the 492-m carbonaceous near-Earth asteroid 2018-12-03. After stationkeeping at ~19 km, it later entered a record orbit 680 m above the surface (930 m from Bennu's centre, June 2019) — the closest spacecraft orbit ever around any celestial body. Spent two years mapping Bennu's boulder-strewn surface and discovering active particle ejections. 2020-10-20 the Touch-and-Go sample arm descended to the Nightingale site, fired N₂ gas into the surface, and grabbed a plume — sinking 50 cm into a 'rubble-pile fluid' surface. Sample Return Capsule delivered 121.6 g of Bennu material to Utah 2023-09-24. The spacecraft itself was immediately redesignated OSIRIS-APEX, en route to a 2029 Apophis rendezvous.
Atlas V 411 from Cape Canaveral SLC-41.

Arrives at Bennu; stationkeeps at ~19 km then progressively tightens to a record orbit 680 m above the surface (930 m from Bennu's centre, June 2019) — closest spacecraft orbit ever around any celestial body.
